translations.Help right ascension: Right ascension (RA): coordinate measured along the celestial equator in hours, minutes and seconds. One turn equals 24 h. Check the reference frame stated in the report.
translations.Help declination: Declination (Dec): angular distance from the celestial equator. Positive north and negative south, in degrees, arcminutes and arcseconds.
translations.Help elongation: Elongation: angular separation between the object and the Sun as seen by the observer. Small values indicate apparent proximity to the Sun in the sky, not a physical distance.
translations.Help phase angle: Phase angle: Sun-object-observer angle, with its vertex at the object. It describes illumination geometry and is different from elongation.
translations.Help tail PA: Tail PA: the antisolar direction projected on the sky, measured east of north. It is a geometric guide for comets, not a prediction of the exact shape or orientation of an observed tail.
translations.Help magnitude: Magnitude: smaller values mean a brighter object. V identifies visual magnitude; T, total comet magnitude. These are estimates and do not guarantee detection under observing conditions.
translations.Help time display: UTC is Coordinated Universal Time. LOCAL uses the reference location’s time zone, including its daylight-saving rules. This choice controls how input dates and times are interpreted. Check each product’s stated time scale: the ephemeris PDF uses UTC.
translations.Help summary reference: The orbital summary is geocentric: its positions and distances use Earth’s center. Local charts use the observing location (topocentric). Differences are expected, especially for nearby objects. The summary can be calculated without an altitude chart.
translations.Help perihelion: Perihelion is the closest passage to the Sun. Normally the summary uses the provider’s osculating perihelion time. For long periods outside the usual window, the period locates the next return and Horizons distances refine the event. An unconfirmed minimum is labeled as estimated.
translations.Help nearest approach: Nearest approach is the smallest Earth distance in the displayed search interval. Normally this is ±365 days from the selected date; for a distant return it is a neighborhood of the next estimated perihelion. Daily samples are refined to 1 minute. This is not a search over the entire orbit.
translations.Help altitude limit: Minimum altitude is the minimum angular height of the object above the horizon for the observing window. The chart uses 5-minute samples; window boundaries and the maximum are sampled.
translations.Help sun limit: Sun limit is the maximum permitted solar altitude. More negative values require a darker sky. Common references: -6° (civil twilight), -12° (nautical) and -18° (astronomical).
translations.Help distance unit: AU is the astronomical unit: 149,597,870.7 km. This preference changes distance display without changing calculations. The summary and its exports use the selected unit.
translations.Summary extended short: Times: {mode}. Next-return search: {start} to {stop}; orbital period ≈ {period} years.
translations.Summary extended conventions: Times: {mode}. The osculating period (≈ {period} years) locates the next return. Horizons distances are searched from {start} to {stop}, around the estimated perihelion, with daily samples refined to 1 minute. The Earth-distance minimum applies only to this interval, not the entire orbit. Event predictions may change with the orbital solution.
translations.Summary perihelion unconfirmed: A perihelion minimum was not confirmed inside this interval; its displayed time is an orbital estimate.
